gloss_terse: completeness, perfection, especially of moral or spiritual maturity
gloss_readable: This term denotes completeness or perfection, particularly in moral and spiritual development. Paul uses it in Colossians to describe love as the bond of perfection that binds all virtues together. In Hebrews, it appears in an exhortation to leave elementary teachings and press on toward maturity. The word emphasizes not just an endpoint but the fullness and wholeness of character that comes through growth.

senses.1: The Greek philosophical and Septuagint background points to completeness of character or development. In Col 3:14, love functions as the perfecting bond that holds all Christian virtues in unity. Heb 6:1 calls believers beyond foundational teachings toward spiritual maturity (τελειότης), suggesting a progressive aspect of perfection rather than instant arrival.

gloss_terse: completion, fulfillment, especially of prophecy, legal instruments, or priestly function
gloss_readable: This word carries the sense of bringing something to its intended completion or fulfillment. The classical usage spans physical completion (buildings, crops reaching ripeness) to legal execution (completing a contract). In Luke 1:45, Mary's Magnificat celebrates the fulfillment of God's promises. Hebrews 7:11 questions whether perfection could come through the Levitical priesthood, pointing toward the need for a superior priestly order in Christ.

senses.1: Drawing on classical meanings of physical completion and legal execution, the New Testament applies τελείωσις to prophetic fulfillment and priestly function. Luke 1:45 celebrates the accomplishment of divine promises to Mary. Heb 7:11's rhetorical question about perfection through the Levitical priesthood highlights the inadequacy of the old covenant and anticipates Christ's superior priesthood bringing true completion.

gloss_terse: Tertullus, a Roman orator hired to prosecute Paul
gloss_readable: Tertullus was a professional orator, likely a Roman or Hellenized advocate, hired by the Jewish leaders to present charges against Paul before Felix. His name is a common Latin diminutive. The flattering speech he delivers in Acts 24 follows typical rhetorical conventions of the period, beginning with elaborate praise of the governor before launching into accusations. His role illustrates the formal legal procedures Paul faced.

senses.1: This proper name appears only in Acts 24:1-2 where the high priest Ananias brings Tertullus as legal counsel to accuse Paul before Governor Felix. The Latin name and rhetorical skill suggest a professional advocate familiar with Roman legal proceedings, hired specifically to present the case in a manner persuasive to Roman authorities.

gloss_terse: forty years old, of forty years' duration
gloss_readable: This adjective describes a span of forty years, whether referring to someone's age or a period of time. In both New Testament occurrences, it marks significant turning points in Israel's history. Moses was forty years old when he attempted to deliver his people (Acts 7:23), and God endured Israel's conduct in the wilderness for a forty-year period (Acts 13:18). The number forty often carries symbolic weight in Scripture, associated with testing, probation, or preparation.

senses.1: The compound adjective (τεσσαρακονταετής) marks forty-year periods with theological significance. Acts 7:23 notes Moses was forty when he first tried to intervene for Israel, while Acts 13:18 recalls God's patient endurance during the forty years of wilderness wandering. Both passages reference foundational periods in Israel's formative history where the forty-year span represented preparation or testing.

gloss_terse: fourteenth, in ordinal sequence
gloss_readable: This ordinal number appears in the dramatic account of Paul's shipwreck voyage, marking the fourteenth night of the storm. The specific time marker heightens the tension and emphasizes how long the crew had endured the tempest without seeing sun or stars, drifting helplessly before making landfall. The detail adds historical precision to Luke's vivid narrative.

senses.1: Both occurrences (Acts 27:27, 33) reference the same dramatic moment: the fourteenth night of Paul's storm-tossed voyage to Rome. The ordinal marks a precise temporal milestone in Luke's detailed shipwreck narrative, emphasizing the prolonged terror and uncertainty the crew faced before finally sensing they were approaching land.

gloss_terse: to punish, avenge, exact retribution
gloss_readable: This verb carries the sense of exacting punishment or vengeance, particularly as an official act of retribution. In classical usage it could describe avenging a slain relative or friend. Paul uses it twice in his defense speeches to describe his former persecution of Christians—he sought to punish them or make them worthy of punishment. The word emphasizes the active pursuit of retribution rather than passive judgment.

senses.1: Drawing from classical usage where τιμωρέω meant to exact vengeance or punishment (often for blood relatives), Paul twice describes his pre-conversion zeal in punishing Christians. In Acts 22:5 and 26:11, the verb captures his active role as a persecutor seeking to bring believers to punishment, not merely approving of their execution but zealously pursuing their condemnation.

gloss_terse: a title, inscription, placard (Latin titulus)
gloss_readable: This Latin loanword refers to an inscription or placard, particularly the type posted above a crucified person to declare the charge against them. John uses it twice to describe the notice Pilate had written and fastened to Jesus' cross: 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.' The inscription was multilingual (Hebrew, Latin, Greek) so all could read it, and its placement over Jesus ironically proclaimed a truth Pilate didn't fully grasp.

senses.1: Borrowed from Latin titulus, this term designates the official inscription posted above a crucifixion victim. Both occurrences (John 19:19-20) refer to the placard Pilate ordered placed on Jesus' cross. The trilingual inscription declared Jesus' identity as King of the Jews, readable by all in the cosmopolitan environment of Jerusalem—an unintended proclamation of truth by a skeptical governor.

gloss_terse: therefore, accordingly, for that very reason
gloss_readable: This strengthened inferential particle draws a conclusion from what precedes. It's more emphatic than simple 'therefore,' carrying the sense of 'for that very reason' or 'well then.' Paul uses it in 1 Thessalonians to connect the Holy Spirit's indwelling with the serious consequences of rejecting sexual purity. Hebrews employs it to draw the conclusion that since we're surrounded by witnesses, we should run our race with endurance.

senses.1: The emphatic particle τοιγαροῦν (a strengthened form of τοιγάρ) appears in 1 Thess 4:8 drawing the weighty conclusion that rejecting moral instruction means rejecting God who gives the Spirit, and in Heb 12:1 inferring from the cloud of witnesses that believers should run with perseverance. Both contexts use the particle to mark a significant logical consequence.

gloss_terse: interest, profit from loaned money
gloss_readable: Though the Greek word originally meant childbirth or offspring, by the Hellenistic period it had developed the financial meaning of interest on money. The metaphorical connection lies in the idea of money 'giving birth' to more money. Both Gospel uses appear in the parable of the talents (or minas), where the master rebukes the fearful servant who didn't even deposit the money with bankers to earn interest.

senses.1: The semantic shift from 'offspring' (classical τόκος) to 'interest' (financial return) reflects the metaphor of money 'bearing' or 'producing' gain. In the parallel passages Matt 25:27 and Luke 19:23, the master chides the unproductive servant who should have at least earned interest (τόκος) by banking the entrusted funds, making the parable's point about minimal expected stewardship.

gloss_terse: to wound, injure violently
gloss_readable: This verb describes inflicting physical wounds or injuries. Luke uses it in the parable of the wicked tenants, where successive servants are wounded and thrown out, and again in the account of the seven sons of Sceva, where the demon-possessed man overpowers them and leaves them wounded and naked. Both contexts emphasize violent physical assault.

senses.1: The verb τραυματίζω denotes violent wounding. In Luke 20:12 (the parable of the tenants), it's the third servant who is wounded and cast out, escalating the violence sequence. Acts 19:16 describes how the demonized man wounded the would-be exorcists (sons of Sceva), demonstrating supernatural strength that left them traumatized—a sobering warning about unauthorized spiritual combat.

gloss_terse: rough, rugged, rocky, jagged
gloss_readable: This adjective describes terrain that is rough, jagged, or difficult to traverse. Luke uses it in quoting Isaiah's prophecy about preparing the Lord's way—rough places shall be made smooth. In Acts, it describes rocky places where the shipwrecked sailors feared being driven and destroyed. The word evokes both physical topography and metaphorical obstacles.

senses.1: From classical usage describing jagged stones or rugged terrain, τραχύς appears in Luke 3:5 quoting Isaiah's highway-preparation prophecy where rough ways (τραχεῖαι) become smooth, symbolizing removing obstacles to God's coming. Acts 27:29 uses it literally for the rocky places (τραχεῖς τόπους) the storm-driven sailors feared would wreck them, adding geographical specificity to the shipwreck narrative.

gloss_terse: three hundred (in number)
gloss_readable: This simple numeral marks an amount in both Gospel accounts: the value in denarii of the precious ointment poured on Jesus. The indignant observers protested this 'waste,' calculating the perfume's worth at nearly a year's wages for a laborer. The specific amount heightens the sense of extravagance and provides historical economic detail.

senses.1: The cardinal number τριακόσιοι appears in the parallel accounts (Mark 14:5, John 12:5) where onlookers value the precious ointment at more than three hundred denarii—representing nearly a full year's wages for a common worker. The precise figure emphasizes the extraordinary cost and the magnitude of the worshipful 'waste' Jesus defends against the critics' economic pragmatism.

gloss_terse: thistles, thorny plants (especially Tribulus terrestris, caltrops)
gloss_readable: This term designates various prickly, thorny plants, particularly the caltrop or puncture vine. In both uses, thistles represent worthless or harmful growth. Jesus uses them in the Sermon on the Mount as an example of bad fruit that reveals a corrupt tree. Hebrews employs them as the negative yield of land that receives God's blessing (rain) but produces thorns instead of crops—land in danger of being cursed.

senses.1: Drawing from botanical terminology for prickly plants like Tribulus terrestris, τρίβολοι symbolize worthless or harmful produce. Matt 7:16 contrasts grapes with thorns and figs with thistles to illustrate how bad trees bear bad fruit. Heb 6:8 uses thistles and thorns as the cursed yield of land that receives rain but fails to produce useful crops—a metaphor for apostate hearts.

gloss_terse: a dish, bowl (for food)
gloss_readable: This word refers to a serving dish or bowl used for food at meals. Both Gospel occurrences appear in the Last Supper narrative, where Jesus identifies his betrayer as 'the one dipping with me in the dish.' The shared dish represents intimate table fellowship, making the betrayal by one who dips from the same bowl all the more poignant and treacherous.

senses.1: From classical usage for cups or bowls, τρύβλιον in Matt 26:23 and Mark 14:20 refers to the common serving dish at the Last Supper. Jesus' statement that his betrayer is 'the one dipping with me in the dish' (τρυβλίῳ) emphasizes the intimate fellowship setting—eating from the same bowl heightened the heinousness of Judas' impending betrayal.

gloss_terse: a hole, especially the eye of a needle
gloss_readable: While this word generally means any bored or drilled hole, in the New Testament it specifically refers to the eye of a needle in Jesus' famous pronouncement about wealth. The image is deliberately hyperbolic—a camel passing through a needle's eye—to emphasize the impossibility of the rich entering God's kingdom by their own power. Some have tried to soften this by inventing a small Jerusalem gate called 'the needle's eye,' but no such gate existed; Jesus meant the literal impossibility.

senses.1: From classical usage for holes in various objects (oar-locks, flutes, gates), τρύπημα/τρῆμα in the parallel sayings (Matt 19:24, Luke 18:25) denotes the eye of a sewing needle (ῥαφίδος). Jesus' image of a camel threading this tiny opening creates a deliberately absurd impossibility to shock his hearers about how wealth hinders entering God's kingdom—human impossibility requiring divine intervention.

gloss_terse: luxury, self-indulgence, voluptuous living
gloss_readable: This noun denotes luxurious living, self-indulgence, or sensual pleasure. It carries negative connotations of softness and excess. Jesus uses it to contrast John the Baptist's ascetic desert life with those who wear soft clothing and live in luxury in kings' palaces. Peter employs it to describe false teachers who count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. The word critiques not wealth itself but self-centered, sensual indulgence.

senses.1: Classical τρυφή ranged from 'delicacy' to 'wantonness' and 'luxuriousness.' Luke 7:25 contrasts John's wilderness existence with those living 'in luxury' (τρυφῇ) in royal courts, highlighting John's prophetic austerity. 2 Pet 2:13 condemns false teachers who 'count reveling in the daytime a pleasure' (τρυφήν), using the term to characterize their self-indulgent, shameless sensuality—living for pleasure rather than godliness.

gloss_terse: glass, crystal, a transparent crystalline material
gloss_readable: Originally referring to rock crystal or crystalline stone, this word came to mean glass by the Hellenistic period. In Revelation's vision of the New Jerusalem, glass appears as a symbol of purity and transparency. The city's street is described as pure gold, yet transparent as glass—a paradoxical image combining supreme value with perfect clarity. The sea of glass before God's throne elsewhere in Revelation evokes both crystalline beauty and the ancient cosmic waters now calm and clear.

senses.1: From classical usage for rock-crystal or crystalline stone, ὕαλος evolved to mean manufactured glass. Both Revelation occurrences (21:18, 21) describe the New Jerusalem's materials: the city is pure gold 'as it were transparent glass' (ὡς ὕαλος διαυγής) and the street is pure gold 'like transparent glass.' The imagery combines preciousness with perfect translucence, suggesting a reality beyond ordinary physical properties.

gloss_terse: one who acts insolently or violently; an arrogant, abusive person
gloss_readable: This term designates someone characterized by violent arrogance, insolence, or abuse of others. It describes more than mere pride—it's aggressive, outward-directed contempt that harms others. Paul uses it in his list of vices marking those who suppress the truth in Romans 1, and again autobiographically, describing his pre-conversion state as a violent persecutor. The word captures the active, harmful dimension of ungodly pride.

senses.1: Classical ὑβριστής described violent, wanton, or insolent persons (like Homer's suitors). Rom 1:30 lists it among the vices of those who reject God—'insolent, arrogant' people who actively harm others. In 1 Tim 1:13, Paul confesses he was formerly an ὑβριστής (violent, insolent man) when persecuting the church, showing how the term denotes aggressive, abusive behavior beyond mere internal pride.

gloss_terse: Hymenaeus, a false teacher who shipwrecked his faith
gloss_readable: Hymenaeus (named after the Greek god of marriage) was a heretical teacher who abandoned sound doctrine and damaged the faith of others. Paul mentions him twice, both times in stark warning. In 1 Timothy, he's one of two men Paul handed over to Satan for discipline so they might learn not to blaspheme. In 2 Timothy, he's linked with Philetus in teaching the resurrection had already happened, thereby upsetting the faith of some believers.

senses.1: This proper name (from the wedding god Hymen) identifies a false teacher appearing in 1 Tim 1:20 and 2 Tim 2:17. Paul 'handed over' Hymenaeus to Satan for discipline after he made shipwreck of faith. Later paired with Philetus, Hymenaeus taught that the resurrection had already occurred, spreading destructive heresy that corrupted believers' understanding of eschatology and undermined hope in bodily resurrection.

gloss_terse: hymns, songs of praise to God
gloss_readable: Hymns are songs composed specifically for worship and praise, particularly addressed to God. Classical usage distinguished hymns (to gods or heroes) from other song types. Paul's instructions in Ephesians and Colossians both mention hymns as part of corporate Spirit-filled worship alongside psalms and spiritual songs. These likely included both inherited Jewish worship forms and new Christian compositions celebrating Christ.

senses.1: From classical designation of songs in praise of gods/heroes, ὕμνοι in Eph 5:19 and Col 3:16 appear in Paul's triad: 'psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.' The three terms (likely overlapping) capture the rich variety of Christian worship music. Hymns specifically may have celebrated Christ's person and work, as suggested by quotations of early christological hymns embedded elsewhere in Paul's letters (e.g., Phil 2:6-11).

gloss_terse: possessions, property, goods, one's substance
gloss_readable: This term refers to one's possessions, property, or material goods—what a person owns. In Acts, it describes the belongings that the early Jerusalem Christians sold to share with those in need, demonstrating radical generosity. In Hebrews, it refers to the earthly possessions that believers joyfully accepted the seizure of, knowing they had better and lasting possessions in heaven. The word highlights the material dimension of ownership that can be either shared or surrendered.

senses.1: From philosophical/logical usage for 'existence' or 'substance,' ὕπαρξις developed the concrete sense of 'possessions' or 'property.' Acts 2:45 describes the Jerusalem believers selling their possessions (ὑπάρξεις) to distribute to the needy. Heb 10:34 commends readers who 'joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions,' knowing heavenly treasures surpass earthly goods—the contrast revealing what holds ultimate value.

gloss_terse: opposed, contrary, hostile, adversarial
gloss_readable: This adjective describes what is set against or opposed to something else—whether enemies in battle, contrary properties, or hostile forces. In Colossians, it qualifies the 'certificate of debt' that stood opposed to us with its legal demands, which Christ canceled. Hebrews uses it to describe the fierce fury of fire that will consume God's adversaries. The word emphasizes active opposition or contrariness.

senses.1: From classical usage for enemies in battle or contrary properties, ὑπεναντίος intensifies simple opposition. Col 2:14 describes the law's handwriting 'that was contrary to us' (ὑπεναντίον ἡμῖν) which Christ removed by nailing to the cross—legal requirements standing as hostile prosecutors. Heb 10:27 warns of 'fury of fire about to consume the adversaries' (τοὺς ὑπεναντίους), using the substantive for God's enemies facing judgment.

gloss_terse: excessive, swollen, bombastic, arrogant (of speech or attitude)
gloss_readable: This adjective describes what is excessively swollen or oversized, and metaphorically, speech that is pompous, bombastic, or boastful. Both New Testament uses describe the inflated, empty words of false teachers. Peter warns of those who speak great swelling words of vanity to entice the unstable. Jude similarly condemns those speaking arrogant words to gain advantage. The image is of puffed-up, hollow rhetoric designed to impress and deceive.

senses.1: From classical usage for excessive bulk or immoderate size, and metaphorically for 'ponderous, verbose' style, ὑπέρογκος describes boastful speech. 2 Pet 2:18 warns of false teachers speaking 'great swelling words' (ὑπέρογκα) of emptiness to seduce the unstable. Jude 16 similarly condemns grumblers speaking 'arrogant words' (ὑπέρογκα) while flattering for advantage—hollow, inflated rhetoric masking spiritual bankruptcy.

gloss_terse: superiority, prominence, pre-eminence, authority
gloss_readable: This noun denotes superiority, prominence, or a position of pre-eminence. Literally it can mean a physical projection or height; metaphorically it indicates excellence or high rank. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians to deny coming with superiority of eloquence or wisdom when proclaiming Christ. In 1 Timothy, it appears in the instruction to pray for those in high positions or authority. The word emphasizes relative status or standing.

senses.1: From classical meanings of physical 'projection' or 'eminence,' ὑπεροχή metaphorically denotes pre-eminence or superiority. 1 Cor 2:1 has Paul disclaiming coming 'with superiority of speech or wisdom' (ὑπεροχὴν λόγου ἢ σοφίας), rejecting rhetorical showmanship. 1 Tim 2:2 instructs prayers 'for those in high position' (ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντων)—those holding authority—showing the term's range from intellectual superiority to official rank.

gloss_terse: to abound exceedingly, overflow greatly, be in excess
gloss_readable: This intensive compound verb means to overflow abundantly or be in extreme excess. Paul uses it to describe both the super-abounding of grace over sin in Romans, and his own overflowing comfort/joy despite affliction in 2 Corinthians. The prefix intensifies the already-strong idea of abounding, suggesting a lavish, almost overwhelming surplus.

senses.1: The compound ὑπερπερισσεύω intensifies περισσεύω (abound) with the prefix ὑπέρ- (beyond, exceedingly). Rom 5:20 declares that where sin increased, grace 'abounded all the more' (ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν)—a theological superlative showing grace's overwhelming victory. 2 Cor 7:4 describes Paul 'overflowing with joy' (ὑπερπερισσεύομαι τῇ χαρᾷ) amid affliction, using the middle voice for abundant internal experience despite external trouble.

gloss_terse: a beast of burden, especially a donkey or ass
gloss_readable: This term originally meant any beast used for yoking or burden-bearing (oxen, mules), but by the Hellenistic period specifically designated donkeys. Matthew uses it in quoting Zechariah's prophecy about the Messiah coming 'seated on a donkey,' fulfilled in Jesus' triumphal entry. Peter employs it in recounting Balaam's rebuke, where a normally speechless donkey spoke to restrain the prophet's madness. Both contexts give theological significance to a humble work animal.

senses.1: From classical 'beast for the yoke' (ὑποζύγιον), the term narrowed to donkeys/asses in later Greek. Matt 21:5 quotes Zechariah 9:9 about the king 'mounted on a donkey' (ἐπὶ ὑποζύγιον), fulfilled when Jesus rode into Jerusalem—the humble beast symbolizing messianic peace versus military conquest. 2 Pet 2:16 recalls Balaam's 'speechless donkey' (ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον) speaking with human voice, the humble animal shaming the mercenary prophet.

gloss_terse: a remnant, what is left remaining
gloss_readable: This term denotes what remains or is left over after others are removed. Paul uses it twice in Romans to describe the faithful remnant of Israel preserved by God's grace. Quoting Isaiah, he notes that though Israel's numbers were like the sand, only a remnant would be saved. Then citing Elijah's experience, Paul reminds readers that even when things seemed hopeless, God preserved 7,000 who hadn't bowed to Baal—a remnant according to the election of grace.

senses.1: From classical usage for what remains or is left behind, ὑπόλειμμα/ὑπολειφθέντες carries theological weight in Paul's remnant theology. Rom 9:27 quotes Isaiah: though Israel's number is vast, 'a remnant will be saved' (τὸ ὑπόλειμμα σωθήσεται). Rom 11:3 cites Elijah's despair ('I alone am left'), before God reveals 7,000 preserved—illustrating that God always maintains a faithful remnant by grace, not human merit.

gloss_terse: to sail under the lee of (an island or coast), seeking shelter from wind
gloss_readable: This nautical term means to sail in the sheltered water on the leeward side of an island or coastline, using the land mass as protection from wind and waves. Luke uses it twice in his detailed account of Paul's voyage to Rome, describing how the storm-battered ship sought refuge by sailing under the lee of Cyprus and then Crete. The technical precision adds authenticity to the narrative.

senses.1: The nautical verb ὑποπλέω describes sailing in the protected waters on the lee side of land. Acts 27:4 and 27:7 both describe the ship's attempt to find shelter during Paul's voyage: sailing 'under the lee of Cyprus' and later Crete because contrary winds prevented direct sailing. Luke's accurate seamanship terminology (reflected across languages: German ὑπεπλεύσαμεν, French naviguer-sous) grounds the narrative in realistic maritime detail.

gloss_terse: to place under, lay down, suggest, propose, risk
gloss_readable: This versatile verb means to place something under or beneath, and by extension to lay down, expose to danger, or put forward as a suggestion. Paul uses it to commend Prisca and Aquila who 'risked their necks' for his life—literally 'placed under' their lives for him. In 1 Timothy, it describes putting these instructions before the brethren or suggesting them. The core meaning of placing beneath extends to various contexts of exposure or presentation.

senses.1: From classical usage for placing items physically underneath or metaphorically categorizing under a class, ὑποτίθημι extends to exposure and suggestion. Rom 16:4 praises Priscilla and Aquila who 'risked their own necks' (τὸν ἑαυτῶν τράχηλον ὑπέθηκαν) for Paul—literally 'placed under' their lives in danger. 1 Tim 4:6 instructs Timothy in 'putting these things before the brothers' (ταῦτα ὑποτιθέμενος), suggesting or reminding them of sound teaching.

gloss_terse: a pattern, example, model, outline
gloss_readable: This term denotes a sketch, outline, or pattern to be followed. In technical writing it could mean a rough draft as opposed to finished work. Paul uses it twice in the Pastoral Epistles to describe exemplary patterns: once referring to himself as a pattern of Christ's patience for future believers, and once urging Timothy to hold to the pattern of sound words Paul taught him. The word emphasizes a normative model worthy of imitation.

senses.1: From classical usage for sketches or outlines (opposed to finished work, ἐξεργασία), ὑποτύπωσις denotes a pattern or model. 1 Tim 1:16 presents Paul as a 'pattern' (ὑποτύπωσιν) of Christ's perfect patience toward future believers—an exemplary case study. 2 Tim 1:13 urges Timothy to 'hold the pattern of sound words' (ὑποτύπωσιν ἔχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων) received from Paul—a normative outline or model of orthodox teaching to preserve and follow.

gloss_terse: to withdraw, retire, go back, retreat
gloss_readable: This verb means to go back, retire, or withdraw from a place or situation. Both Gospel uses describe Jesus withdrawing from crowds or situations to seek solitude. In Luke 5, after healing a leper and facing growing crowds, Jesus withdrew to desolate places to pray. In Luke 9, he withdrew from Herod's territory after the feeding of the 5,000. The pattern shows Jesus' rhythm of ministry and withdrawal for communion with the Father.

senses.1: Classical ὑποχωρέω described retiring or withdrawing (often in military contexts or giving way). Luke employs it for Jesus' strategic withdrawals: Luke 5:16 notes he 'would withdraw to desolate places and pray' (ὑποχωρῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις), creating space for prayer amid mounting popularity. Luke 9:10 has Jesus withdrawing privately (ὑπεχώρησεν) after the 5,000's feeding—both passages showing Jesus' deliberate rhythm of public ministry and private renewal.

gloss_terse: to strike under the eye, give a black eye; metaphorically: to discipline harshly, wear out with demands
gloss_readable: Literally meaning to strike someone under the eye (giving a black eye), this verb developed metaphorical uses for harsh treatment. Jesus uses it in the parable of the persistent widow who keeps bothering the unjust judge, saying she will 'wear him out' with her constant coming. Paul employs it for his rigorous self-discipline, treating his body harshly like a boxer pummeling an opponent, lest he be disqualified after preaching to others.

senses.1: From the literal sense 'strike under the eye' (giving a black eye), ὑπωπιάζω extends metaphorically to harsh treatment. Luke 18:5 has the persistent widow threatening to 'wear out' the judge (ὑπωπιάζῃ με) with her relentless coming—either exhausting him or potentially shaming him publicly. 1 Cor 9:27 describes Paul 'disciplining' his body harshly (ὑπωπιάζω), using boxing imagery of striking blows, to maintain self-control and avoid disqualification after preaching to others.

gloss_terse: hyssop, a plant used in purification rituals (possibly Origanum hirtum)
gloss_readable: Hyssop was a plant used throughout Scripture for ritual purification and sprinkling. The exact botanical identification is debated (possibly marjoram or Syrian oregano rather than modern hyssop), but it had bushy branches suitable for sprinkling liquids. In John's Gospel, a sponge soaked with sour wine is put on hyssop and lifted to Jesus on the cross. Hebrews mentions Moses using hyssop to sprinkle blood during the covenant ceremony. Both recall Passover and purification rituals.

senses.1: Hebrew אֵזוֹב rendered as ὕσσωπος designates the purification plant (possibly Origanum hirtum). John 19:29 describes the wine-soaked sponge placed 'on hyssop' (ὑσσώπῳ) and lifted to Jesus—recalling Passover's hyssop for blood application and adding symbolic depth to crucifixion details. Heb 9:19 mentions Moses sprinkling blood 'with hyssop' in covenant ratification, linking old covenant purification rites to Christ's superior sacrifice.

gloss_terse: lack, need, deficiency, what is lacking
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a lack, deficiency, or what is missing. It can refer to material poverty or any shortage. Mark uses it to describe the poor widow who gave from her poverty—literally 'from her lack.' Paul employs it in Philippians when discussing his contentment, having learned to be satisfied whether in abundance or in want. The word emphasizes the state of need or insufficiency.

senses.1: The noun ὑστέρημα (related to ὑστερέω, 'fall short, lack') denotes deficiency or need. Mark 12:44 describes the widow giving 'from her poverty' (ἐκ τῆς ὑστερήσεως αὐτῆς)—literally her lack or want—making her two coins more significant than the rich's surplus. Phil 4:11 (variant reading: some have ὑστέρησιν) connects to Paul's learned contentment 'in whatever state'—including states of need versus abundance.

gloss_terse: height, high position; metaphorically: exaltation, lofty thing
gloss_readable: This term denotes physical height or elevation, and metaphorically, exaltation or anything that exalts itself. Paul uses it in Romans' famous declaration that nothing in creation—including height or depth—can separate believers from God's love. In 2 Corinthians, he employs it for every lofty thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, which must be torn down. The word captures both spatial and prideful dimensions of height.

senses.1: From classical usage for elevation or height (including astronomical exaltation), ὕψωμα appears in Rom 8:39's cosmic catalog: neither 'height nor depth' (ὕψωμα οὔτε βάθος) can separate from God's love—likely spatial/cosmological powers. 2 Cor 10:5 uses it metaphorically for 'every lofty thing' (πᾶν ὕψωμα) exalting itself against knowing God—proud arguments or strongholds requiring demolition. The semantic range spans physical elevation to arrogant self-exaltation.

gloss_terse: a glutton, one who eats excessively
gloss_readable: This simple noun designates a glutton or excessive eater. Both Gospel uses appear in the same accusation Jesus quotes: his critics called him 'a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.' The charge was false but revealed the religious establishment's contempt for Jesus' table fellowship with outcasts. Unlike John the Baptist's asceticism, Jesus' eating and drinking with sinners scandalized the self-righteous.

senses.1: The noun φάγος (from φαγεῖν, 'to eat') denotes a glutton. Both occurrences (Matt 11:19, Luke 7:34) quote the identical slander against Jesus: 'Behold, a glutton and drunkard' (φάγος καὶ οἰνοπότης)—contrasting him unfavorably with John's asceticism. The false accusation revealed critics' rejection: John was too austere (demon-possessed), Jesus too convivial (glutton). Either way, they refused God's messengers.

gloss_terse: manifestation, disclosure, making visible or known
gloss_readable: This noun denotes the act of manifesting, revealing, or making something visible that was previously hidden. Paul uses it for the manifestation of the Spirit given to each believer for the common good—spiritual gifts are visible evidences of the Spirit's presence. In 2 Corinthians, he speaks of the manifestation of truth, openly commending himself to every conscience by making truth plainly visible. The word emphasizes making the hidden apparent.

senses.1: From φανερόω ('make visible, manifest'), φανέρωσις denotes disclosure or manifestation. 1 Cor 12:7 describes 'the manifestation of the Spirit' (φανέρωσις τοῦ πνεύματος) given to each for common benefit—spiritual gifts as visible evidences of the Spirit's presence and activity. 2 Cor 4:2 speaks of Paul's ministry 'by manifestation of the truth' (φανερώσει τῆς ἀληθείας) commending himself to all consciences—making truth openly visible versus hidden cunning.

gloss_terse: an apparition, ghost, phantom
gloss_readable: This word denotes a phantom, ghost, or apparition—something that appears but lacks physical substance. Both Gospel uses describe the disciples' terrified reaction when they saw Jesus walking on water. In the darkness and storm, they thought they were seeing a ghost and cried out in fear. The word captures their interpretation before recognizing it was actually Jesus performing a nature miracle.

senses.1: From φαντάζω ('make visible'), φάντασμα denotes an apparition or phantom. The parallel accounts (Matt 14:26, Mark 6:49) describe the disciples seeing Jesus walking on the sea and thinking 'it is a ghost' (φάντασμά ἐστιν)—crying out in terror. Their fear of a phantom reveals both the darkness and storm's disorientation and their not yet comprehending Jesus' divine power over nature. His 'It is I' reassures them of his real, physical presence.

gloss_terse: sorcery, magic arts, use of drugs or spells
gloss_readable: This term originally meant the use of drugs (whether medicinal or toxic), but developed the sense of sorcery, magic arts, or witchcraft—often associated with potions and spells. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh in Galatians. Revelation uses it to describe how Babylon the Great deceived all nations with her sorceries. The word connects pharmakological manipulation with occult practices, both involving spiritual deception.

senses.1: From φάρμακον ('drug, potion'), φαρμακεία evolved from drug-use to sorcery/witchcraft (often involving potions and spells). Gal 5:20 lists 'sorcery' (φαρμακεία) among fleshly works opposed to the Spirit—occult practices incompatible with Kingdom life. Rev 18:23 explains Babylon deceived all nations 'by your sorcery' (ἐν τῇ φαρμακείᾳ σου)—magical arts tied to her seductive, idolatrous commerce and spiritual adultery.

gloss_terse: sparingly, stingily, grudgingly
gloss_readable: This adverb means sparingly, grudgingly, or in a stingy manner. Paul uses it twice in the same verse in 2 Corinthians to establish the principle of sowing and reaping: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, but whoever sows generously will reap generously. The word captures the tight-fisted, reluctant attitude in giving that limits both the gift and the eventual return.

senses.1: The adverb φειδομένως (from φείδομαι, 'spare, refrain') denotes sparing or grudging action. Both uses in 2 Cor 9:6 establish the agricultural metaphor for giving: 'The one sowing sparingly (φειδομένως) will also reap sparingly (φειδομένως), and the one sowing bountifully will reap bountifully.' The doubled adverb emphasizes the direct proportion: stingy sowing yields meager harvest, generous sowing yields abundant return.
